Layout Ideas for a Small Game Room

Getting the layout right is the single most important step when you're working with a small games room. The goal is to keep the floor as clear as possible so the room doesn't feel cluttered the moment you walk in.

Push furniture against walls wherever you can, and think carefully about traffic flow — you need to be able to move around the room comfortably, especially if it's a multiplayer space. I always sketch out a rough floor plan first, even just on paper, before moving a single piece of furniture.

[[IMG|small-games-room-layout-ideas|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A compact games room with furniture pushed neatly to the walls, a small sofa or loveseat facing a wall-mounted screen, a fold-away table in the corner, open shelving for board games, and a neatly arranged console setup. The floor is clear, with a low-pile rug anchoring the seating area. Warm neutral tones, mid-century furniture touches, natural wood accents. A young Black man in a relaxed casual pose is sitting on the sofa, controller in hand, glancing towards the camera with a natural smile.]]

Layout principles that actually work in a small space

  • Zone by activity: Separate your gaming screen area from any board game table, even with just a rug or change of lighting.
  • Wall-mount your screen: This frees up an entire surface and makes the room feel less cluttered instantly.
  • Go corner-first: Corner desks and corner shelving units make the most of awkward angles without eating into the centre of the room.
  • Use a loveseat, not a full sofa: A two-seater is usually plenty and keeps proportions in check.
  • Keep the doorway clear: Never block the natural sightline when you open the door — it immediately makes the room feel boxed-in.
  • Choose round or oval tables: For board game tables, rounded edges mean fewer bruised hips and a less rigid feel.

I once helped a client in a Victorian terraced house who had a narrow third bedroom — barely enough for a single bed. We turned it into a two-person gaming den by wall-mounting the TV, adding a floating shelf for the console, and fitting a compact loveseat on castors so it could roll back easily. The room felt twice as big once the floor was clear.

Pro Tip: Measure your room before buying anything. It sounds obvious, but I've seen clients buy the perfect sofa only to find it blocks the door. Take the room's measurements with you when you shop.

Storage and Furniture That Save Space

In a small games room, furniture has to work harder than it does anywhere else in the house. Every piece should ideally serve at least two purposes — a storage ottoman is better than a coffee table, a desk with drawers beats a plain surface, and wall shelving beats a freestanding unit every time.

The mistake I see most often is clients filling a small room with too many pieces of furniture, each doing just one job. Strip it back and choose less, but choose better.

[[IMG|space-saving-furniture-games-room|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A small games room with smart space-saving furniture: a wall-mounted floating shelf holding a games console and controllers, a storage ottoman doubling as seating with the lid open to show board games inside, a fold-flat wall-mounted table, and a slim pegboard on the wall with accessories hung neatly. Warm wood tones and sage green accents. A South Asian woman in her 30s is opening the ottoman storage, smiling, in a natural candid moment.]]

Best space-saving furniture choices for small games rooms

Furniture Piece Why It Works What to Avoid
Storage ottoman Seating + storage in one; hides controllers, cables, card decks Oversized versions that dominate the room
Floating shelves Store games vertically without using floor space Shelves that are too deep — 20–25 cm is usually plenty
Wall-mounted fold-down table Folds away when not in use; great for board games Cheap fixings — always use wall anchors
Corner desk unit Uses dead corner space efficiently for PC gaming L-shapes that are too large for the room
Pegboard wall panel Customisable storage for controllers, headsets, accessories Going too small — a larger pegboard looks more intentional
Loveseat on castors Easily repositioned for multiplayer setups Bulky three-seater sofas that eat floor space
[[PRODUCT|compact storage ottoman with lid for games room]]
Pro Tip: A pegboard is one of the most underrated pieces of games room storage. Paint it to match your wall colour and it looks like a deliberate design feature rather than an afterthought.

Wall Art and Wall Decor Ideas Specifically for Small Game Rooms

This is the section I get most excited about — because wall art is genuinely one of the fastest ways to transform a small games room from a cramped spare room into something with real personality. Good game room art ideas don't just fill blank walls; they set the tone for the whole space.

The question I always ask clients is: what feeling do you want when you walk in here? Retro arcade energy? Sleek modern gaming aesthetic? Relaxed board game lounge vibe? Your answer should shape every art choice you make.

[[IMG|game-room-art-ideas-wall-decor|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (product images show the art). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — floating shelves, wall-mounted sconces, a macramé hanging, a pegboard, a mirror — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A small but characterful games room wall styled with floating shelves holding board games and small plants, a neon wall sconce, a pegboard with accessories, and decorative items on the shelves. The palette is deep navy and warm wood, with pops of amber from the lighting. A mixed-race couple in their late 20s are standing by the shelves together, the man pointing at something on the shelf while the woman laughs.]]

Game room art ideas that actually work

  • Retro gaming prints: Classic arcade-style illustrations or pixel art prints add nostalgia and character without feeling childish — these work brilliantly for adults too.
  • Board game wall art: Oversized prints inspired by chess, Scrabble tiles, dice, or playing card suits make brilliant statement pieces in a board game lounge setup.
  • Abstract prints in bold colours: If you want a sleeker look, bold geometric abstracts complement a modern gaming setup without competing with your screens.
  • Map prints: Fantasy maps, world maps, or city maps work brilliantly in a games room — particularly if you're a fan of strategy or RPG games.
  • Typography prints: A print with a quote that means something to you — game-related or otherwise — adds personality without being too literal.
  • Gallery walls: Mix a few smaller prints in a cohesive colour palette to fill a wall without overpowering the space. Keep the frames the same colour for a tidy look.
[[PRODUCT|retro gaming wall art prints for a games room]]

One client of mine was a huge board game enthusiast — she had shelves of games but bare white walls. We added a large-scale print inspired by a vintage board game aesthetic alongside a gallery wall of chess and playing card themed artwork. The room went from "storage cupboard with a table" to a proper games lounge almost overnight.

Real Example: Board game wall art works especially well in a neutral-toned room. Keep the walls pale and let the artwork carry the colour — it's far more effective than painting everything dark and then struggling to find art that fits.
[[PRODUCT|board game themed art prints for home decor]]

How to Use Vertical Wall Space and Murals to Make a Small Room Feel Larger

When floor space is limited, the walls become your best friend. Using vertical space cleverly — through tall shelving, high-hung art, and wall murals — can make a small games room feel significantly bigger than it is.

The trick is to draw the eye upwards. When someone walks into a room and their gaze immediately moves up, their brain reads the space as taller and more expansive. It genuinely works.

[[IMG|vertical-wall-space-games-room-mural|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top, then a clear VISUAL comparison (two labelled photos side by side, or simple labelled icons/steps), minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks. Show two side-by-side labelled small room illustrations: LEFT labelled "Before: Low Art, Cluttered Floor" showing a small room with low-hung decor and furniture crowding the floor. RIGHT labelled "After: Tall Shelves, High Art, Wall Mural" showing the same room with tall floating shelves, art hung high on the wall, and a large-scale mural creating depth — the room reads as much larger and airier.]]

How to maximise vertical space in a small games room

  • Hang art higher than you think: Most people hang art at eye level, but in a small room, hanging a piece 10–15 cm higher than usual draws the eye up and raises the perceived ceiling height.
  • Use floor-to-ceiling shelving: This is one of the most dramatic transformations you can make — it uses every centimetre of vertical space and looks incredible.
  • Try a feature wall mural: A large-scale mural — an abstract landscape, a geometric pattern, or a sci-fi cityscape — creates a sense of depth that a single colour simply can't. The eye reads it as distance.
  • Vertical stripes or linear patterns: Whether it's wallpaper, a painted stripe, or a series of tall vertical prints, vertical lines literally make walls look taller.
  • Go tall with your curtains: If you have a window, hang curtains from as close to the ceiling as possible, even if the window is small. This makes the entire wall feel taller.
  • Use mirrors strategically: A large mirror on a side wall can effectively double the perceived size of the room. A round mirror at eye level reads as a design feature, not just a trick.
Pro Tip: If you're not ready to commit to a full wall mural, try a large single-panel print in an oversized format — something that takes up most of a wall. The effect is similar and it's much easier to change later.

Colour Psychology for Gaming Rooms and How Wall Colour Affects Gameplay Mood

Colour is one of the most powerful tools in any room design, and in a games room it matters more than most people realise. The colours on your walls genuinely influence how alert, relaxed, or focused you feel while you play.

I'm not talking about anything mystical here — this is straightforward psychology that interior designers use every day. Getting the colour right is completely free if you're repainting anyway, so it's worth thinking about seriously.

[[IMG|gaming-room-colour-psychology-wall-colour|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "How Wall Colour Affects Gaming Room Mood", then a clear visual comparison showing four colour swatches in a row — deep navy blue, forest green, charcoal grey, and warm terracotta — each with a short label beneath: "Focus & Calm", "Natural & Grounding", "Sleek & Dramatic", "Energised & Social". Minimal text, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Choosing the right wall colour for your games room

  • Deep navy or midnight blue: Brilliant for video gaming dens — it's immersive and reduces eye strain by cutting harsh contrast between a bright screen and a bright wall.
  • Charcoal or dark grey: Sleek and modern, works well for adult gaming setups, especially with LED accent lighting. Makes colours on screen pop beautifully.
  • Forest or sage green: An increasingly popular choice — grounding and calming, and it pairs beautifully with natural wood tones for a less "tech bunker" feel.
  • Warm terracotta or rust: Great for social game rooms designed around board games and conversation — energising and warm without being aggressive.
  • White or very pale grey: The safest choice for a small room, as it bounces light and makes the space feel bigger. Layer in colour through your art and decor instead.
  • Avoid: Bright red or orange on all four walls — stimulating to the point of being tiring for long gaming sessions.

A client once asked me to help redesign her teenage son's gaming room, which was painted a very bright, slightly aggressive lime green. He complained he felt agitated after long sessions. We repainted in a deep navy, added warm LED strip lighting behind the desk, and the difference in how he described the room — "calmer but still cool" — was immediate. Colour really does matter.

Pro Tip: If you're unsure about committing to a dark wall colour, paint one feature wall first and live with it for a week. Dark colours almost always look better than you expect — they add depth, not gloom.

Lighting, Sound and Decor on a Budget

A games room doesn't need an enormous budget to look and feel great. In fact, lighting is one of the cheapest and most impactful upgrades you can make — and it makes a far bigger difference than most people expect.

Sound is worth thinking about too, especially in a small room where things can get loud. A few simple, affordable fixes can make the space far more usable and enjoyable.

[[IMG|games-room-lighting-budget-decor|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — floating shelves, wall sconces, a neon-effect sign, macramé, pegboard — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A small games room glowing warmly at dusk, lit by LED strip lighting behind a floating desk, a small floor lamp in the corner, and a wall sconce above a shelf. The room feels cosy and atmospheric. Budget-friendly decor — plants on shelves, a colourful rug, a pegboard with accessories. A young white woman in her mid-20s is adjusting the LED strip behind the desk, looking pleased, in a natural candid pose.]]

Budget lighting, sound and decor ideas for a small games room

  • LED strip lighting: Run these behind a desk, under shelves, or along a skirting board for instant atmosphere. Available in a huge range of colours and dimmable options.
  • A single good floor lamp: One warm-toned floor lamp in a corner transforms the mood of a small room for very little money.
  • Foam panels or acoustic tiles: If sound is an issue, acoustic foam panels on a wall absorb echo. They come in various shapes and can look like a deliberate design choice.
  • Rugs for sound dampening: A thick rug on the floor absorbs sound as well as defining the seating zone. Two jobs, one purchase.
  • Plants: A few low-maintenance plants — a spider plant, a pothos, a small succulent collection — add life and colour for very little outlay.
  • DIY neon sign effect: LED neon flex can be bent into shapes or words and mounted on a wall — a far cheaper alternative to real glass neon, and genuinely effective.
[[PRODUCT|LED floor lamp for gaming room ambience]] [[PRODUCT|thick woven rug for games room sound and style]]
Pro Tip: Layered lighting — meaning three or more different light sources at different heights — always makes a room feel more considered and designed. Even if each individual light is cheap, the combination looks expensive.

Small Game Room Ideas for Adults, Kids and Rooms with a Bed

The best small game room ideas will look quite different depending on who the room is for and how it's being used. An adult gaming den needs different things to a kids' games room, and a games room with a bed in it is a whole different challenge again.

Let me break down the approach for each, because the design decisions really do diverge quite significantly.

[[IMG|small-game-room-adults-kids-bed|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A split-scene composition showing two adjoining small rooms: one side is an adult gaming den with a sleek dark palette, a wall-mounted screen, pegboard with controllers, and moody LED lighting; the other side is a bright children's games room with colourful shelving, a bean bag, a chalkboard wall section, and a playful rug. A Black father is kneeling beside a young child on the kids' side, smiling, in a natural warm pose.]]

Game room decor for adults

  • Go dark and moody — deep navy, charcoal or forest green walls with warm accent lighting create an immersive atmosphere.
  • Keep the decor minimal and intentional — a few well-chosen art prints, a good chair, and tidy cable management go further than lots of clutter.
  • Invest in seating — an adult gaming den is only as good as the chair or sofa you spend hours in. This is where it's worth spending a bit more.
  • Use wall art to add personality without filling the room with stuff — a large statement print or a small gallery wall is far better than shelves of knick-knacks.

Kids' games room ideas

  • Prioritise durability and ease of cleaning — wipeable surfaces and washable rugs are non-negotiable.
  • Use colour boldly but with a plan — stick to two or three colours maximum so it feels fun but not chaotic.
  • Include a chalkboard wall or section — kids love it, it's cheap, and it doubles as creative play space.
  • Keep storage at child height so they can actually put things away themselves (wildly optimistic, I know, but worth a try).

Games room with a bed (guest room / studio)

  • A sofa bed or day bed is your best friend here — it functions as extra seating during gaming and converts for overnight guests.
  • Use curtains or a room divider to separate the sleeping area from the gaming area, even loosely.
  • Keep the gaming setup compact and wall-mounted so the bed area doesn't feel overwhelmed.
  • Choose calmer, more neutral decor than you would for a dedicated gaming den — it needs to feel restful too.
[[PRODUCT|gaming artwork prints for adult games room decor]]
Pro Tip: For a games room that also has a bed, treat the two zones as separate rooms in terms of mood — different lighting circuits, a different rug or flooring treatment, and slightly different decor on each side. The contrast actually makes both areas feel more purposeful.

Budget Small Game Room Transformations: Before and After Examples

Some of the best small game room transformations I've been involved in cost very little. The biggest improvements almost never come from expensive furniture — they come from clearing clutter, adding a lick of paint, and putting up the right decor.

Let me walk you through a couple of realistic before-and-after scenarios that show exactly what's possible on a tight budget.

[[IMG|budget-games-room-before-after-transformation|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Small Games Room Budget Transformation". Then a clear VISUAL comparison: two labelled room illustrations side by side — LEFT labelled "Before" showing a small cluttered room with flat overhead lighting, boxes on the floor, blank white walls, and a TV on a bulky freestanding unit. RIGHT labelled "After" showing the same room transformed: wall-mounted TV, floating shelves with board games, a pegboard for accessories, LED strip lighting creating atmosphere, a colourful rug anchoring the seating, and a small plant on a shelf. Minimal text, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

What a typical budget games room transformation looks like

  • Before: Bare white walls, clutter on the floor, overhead light only, bulky TV stand eating floor space, no defined zones.
  • Step 1 — Clear and paint: Remove everything unnecessary, then repaint the main wall in a deeper, warmer colour. Cost: very low.
  • Step 2 — Wall-mount the screen: A TV wall bracket is inexpensive and immediately reclaims the floor space the TV unit was taking up.
  • Step 3 — Add floating shelves: Two or three shelves replace a freestanding unit and display games and decor neatly.
  • Step 4 — Introduce a rug: A good-sized rug anchors the seating area, adds warmth, and defines the zone.
  • Step 5 — Layer the lighting: Replace the single overhead light with a lamp and LED strips behind the desk or shelves.
  • Step 6 — Hang art: One to three well-chosen prints on the wall transform the feel of the entire space for relatively little money.
  • After: The same room feels twice as big, intentional, and genuinely enjoyable to spend time in.

I helped a friend do exactly this in a box room behind her kitchen. Total spend was under what she'd originally budgeted for a new sofa alone. She had a fully functional, genuinely stylish games lounge within a weekend. The wall art and lighting made the biggest visible difference.

Real Example: The single most impactful change in almost every budget games room transformation I've seen is replacing a bulky freestanding TV unit with a wall-mounted screen and floating shelves. It immediately gives the impression of a room that's been properly designed, not just furnished.

DIY Games Room Home Decor Ideas

DIY games room home decor is one of my favourite topics, because it lets you get a genuinely unique result for a fraction of the cost of buying everything new. And honestly, some of the most characterful games rooms I've ever seen were almost entirely DIY.

The key is knowing which DIY projects are worth your time and which are likely to look homemade in the bad sense of the word. Here's my honest take.

[[IMG|diy-games-room-home-decor-ideas|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — a DIY pegboard, handmade macramé hanging, painted shelves, a chalkboard section of wall — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A small games room styled with clearly DIY but beautifully finished home decor: a painted wooden pegboard with controllers hung on hooks, a macramé wall hanging above a shelf, a chalkboard section of wall with a score chart on it, and neatly stencilled shelving. Warm afternoon light. A young mixed-race woman in her late 20s is painting a small shelf at a workbench in the corner, focused and happy, in a natural candid pose.]]

DIY decor ideas that actually look good

  • Painted pegboard: Buy a standard pegboard sheet, paint it in your chosen colour, and mount it. Add hooks and shelves for a fully customised storage and display wall. Looks far better than a plain bought version.
  • DIY neon sign: LED neon flex mounted on a piece of painted MDF makes a surprisingly professional-looking wall feature. You can spell out a word or create a simple shape.
  • Chalkboard wall section: Paint one section of wall with chalkboard paint for a scoreboard, doodle space, or just to add texture. Great in both adult and kids' games rooms.
  • Printed and framed art: Find a high-resolution image you love, print it at a large format print shop, and frame it yourself. For a fraction of the cost of a ready-made print, you can get something genuinely unique.
  • Macramé wall hanging: Simple beginner macramé patterns are surprisingly quick to learn and add great texture to a games room wall. Dozens of tutorials online.
  • Repainted and rearranged shelving: Take plain flat-pack shelves and paint them in a bold accent colour before mounting. Instantly more characterful than the factory finish.
  • DIY controller holder: A strip of wooden dowels or hooks mounted on a painted plank makes a tidy, good-looking wall-mounted controller rack.
Pro Tip: The difference between DIY decor that looks great and DIY decor that looks cheap almost always comes down to finish. Take the extra time to sand, prime, and paint properly. A well-finished DIY piece looks deliberately made; a rushed one just looks unfinished.

Mistakes That Make a Small Game Room Feel Smaller

I've walked into a lot of small games rooms over the years, and there are a handful of mistakes I see again and again that make a small space feel genuinely cramped. The good news is that every single one of these is fixable.

Some of these will seem obvious once I point them out — but they're extremely common, which is why they're on this list.

The most common small games room mistakes

  • Too much furniture: Every extra piece you squeeze in shrinks the feeling of the room. Be ruthless — only keep what genuinely earns its place.
  • Overhead lighting only: A single ceiling light casts flat, harsh light that makes a room feel smaller and less inviting. Layer your lighting sources.
  • Art hung too low: Hanging art at standard eye level in a small room is a wasted opportunity. Hang higher to draw the eye up and add perceived height.
  • Ignoring cables: Trailing cables on the floor make even a beautiful room look messy. Invest in cable management — it's cheap and makes an enormous difference.
  • Going too dark with no light sources: Dark walls look brilliant, but only if you balance them with enough warm light. Without it, you get a cave, not a den.
  • Matching everything too precisely: A room where every piece of furniture is from the same range often looks more flat and boxed-in than one with a thoughtful mix.
  • Neglecting the ceiling: Paint the ceiling the same colour as the walls (or one shade lighter) to remove the visual "lid" effect that makes low ceilings feel even lower.
  • Skipping the rug: Without a rug, a small room often feels like it has too much hard floor. A rug zones the space and makes it feel finished.
Pro Tip: If your games room feels smaller than it should, start by removing things rather than adding things. Decluttering and cable management alone can transform the perceived size of a room before you spend a penny on new decor.
